risks: Silica fiber cannot transmit MIR wavelengths – signal loss would prevent measurement.
High temperature or aggressive chemicals in the petroleum line could degrade chalcogenide fiber if not properly protected.
If the oil is highly scattering, ATR coupling may be limited; probe fouling could affect repeatability.
The mid-IR fibre link over the required distance is not shown to be feasible in the supplied material.

steps: Measure the transmission of the chosen mid-IR fibre over the planned link length, or plan the analyzer close to the measurement point.
Obtain a short chalcogenide fiber segment and connect it to a laboratory FTIR to verify transmission of water‑containing oil samples.
Build a calibration set of petroleum samples with known water concentrations (reference gravimetric or Karl Fischer method).
Develop a chemometric model on laboratory data, validate on held‑out samples.
Install the ATR probe in a pilot line, use the chalcogenide fiber of the planned length, and compare online predictions to reference measurements.
Evaluate signal loss, temperature effects, and probe fouling over typical operating periods.

assumptions: The petroleum stream is optically clear enough for ATR contact (no heavy scattering).
A suitable chalcogenide fiber can be sourced and installed within the plant’s safety and routing constraints.
Reference water‑content measurements are available for model building.

MIR‑ATR with chalcogenide (As‑S) fiber: Chalcogenide fibers transmit the 2.5–6.5 µm range needed for MIR‑ATR, unlike silica fibers which stop at ~2.4 µm; this matches the absorption bands of water in petroleum. (not supported by the cited page)

NIR transmission probe (as fallback): If a suitable MIR fiber cannot be installed, NIR can monitor water indirectly via overtone bands, using the existing silica fiber; however, sensitivity is lower for low water levels. (not supported by the cited page)
pointsToConfirm: Maximum allowable fiber length and bend radius for the chosen chalcogenide cable.
Temperature and chemical compatibility of the chalcogenide fiber with the process environment.
Exact optical appearance (clarity, scattering) of the oil at the measurement location.
